extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, mathematicians, and educated readers interested in probability, induction, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to estimate probabilities, infer causes from observed effects, and decide when coincidences warrant accepting empirical laws. Covers prerequisites for applying probability, the role of causal knowledge versus observed frequency, Bayes-like reasoning, and limits on extrapolating empirical (derivative) laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for classical probability calculation (Laplace)
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate chances by the classical method two things are necessary: we must know that of several events some one will certainly happen, and no more than one; and we must not know, nor have any reason to expect, that it will be one of these events rather than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace’s formulation: reduce events to equally possible cases and take the ratio of favourable cases to all possible cases as the measure of probability. These prerequisites are essential before applying the simple counting-based calculus of chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification required for assuming equal probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling two events 'equally probable' requires either specific experience showing they occur equally often or deductive grounds (e.g. physical symmetry) for expecting equal frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may justify equal odds either by experiment, by everyday experience of similar events, or deductively from mechanical/symmetry arguments (e.g. a symmetric coin). Absent such justification, treating events as equally likely is not warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability is degree of belief conditional on available evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability is not an intrinsic property of the event but a measure of the ground we have for expecting it; it changes with evidence and is relative to the observer’s knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: knowing only a name gives one probability; learning the person is terminally ill changes that probability. Thus probabilities should be updated as new evidence arrives; they differ across observers or as evidence accumulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting 'as if' under ignorance does not imply the world is symmetric
rubrics_metrics.description: When forced to choose with no information except the set of possible mutually exclusive outcomes, it is rational to act as if outcomes were equally likely (e.g. bet as though the box has equal numbers), but this is a pragmatic stance, not a claim that the underlying frequencies are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The option of indifference guides conduct in ignorance but should not be mistaken for evidence of actual equality of cases; if additional information appears it should change the probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer improving empirical data over elaborate probabilistic calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight improvement in the quality or relevance of data is often more valuable than complex probabilistic manipulation of poor data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying the calculus of probabilities to a problem, obtain the best attainable positive knowledge (comparative frequencies or causal information). Misapplication of formal probability to weak data has produced serious errors (e.g. naive computations about witnesses or juries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying wide averages to individual cases where case-specific factors dominate
rubrics_metrics.description: Population averages (general ratios) are of limited value for judging individual instances, especially when individual cases may differ widely from the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating witnesses or particular legal cases, consider case-specific factors (consistency, behavior under cross-examination, interests, mental capacity) rather than relying solely on a crude ratio of true to false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware independence assumptions when aggregating judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning that increasing the number of judges will necessarily reduce the chance of error assumes individual errors are independent; common causes of error or shared biases can make increased numbers worsen or fail to improve correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that majority aggregation eliminates error; consider moral and psychological effects of enlarging tribunals and possible correlated errors across judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilities grounded on causal knowledge are superior to those from mere frequency counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating probability by understanding and estimating frequencies of the causes (causal analysis) gives a firmer basis than simple empirical counting of effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, ascend from effects to causes and estimate how often causes favorable/unfavorable to the effect occur. Causal-grounded probabilities correct or confirm empirical frequency-based estimates and are a higher-order datum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid induction is required to legitimize frequency-based probability estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: When probability is taken as the ratio of cases in which an event occurs to all cases of that description, this rests on an induction (per enumerationem simplicem) that must be valid for the calculation to be legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that empirical probabilities derived from observation are themselves inductive generalizations; ensure the induction is appropriate (sufficiently representative samples, relevant conditions) before using the fraction as a probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace’s Sixth Principle (ascending from events to causes / Bayesian core)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an effect and several possible causes, the probability that a particular cause produced the effect is proportional to the antecedent probability of that cause multiplied by the probability that the cause, if present, would have produced the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in three illustrative cases: (I) causes equal in producing effect but different antecedent frequencies — ratio follows antecedent probabilities; (II) antecedents equal but different efficacies — ratio follows comparative efficacies; (III) general case — probability proportional to the product prior×likelihood. Use this rule when inferring causes from observed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for probability of repeated independent coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the probability of a single casual coincidence is 1/m, the probability that the same coincidence will be repeated n times in succession (assuming independence) is 1/m^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to calculate how rapidly the chance hypothesis diminishes with repeated identical outcomes (e.g. repeated dice throws). Use this to help decide whether repeated occurrences are plausibly accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare antecedent probabilities when deciding between chance and causal hypotheses for coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether an observed series of coincidences is due to chance or to causation, compare the antecedent probability of the chance combination with the antecedent probability of the causal hypothesis; the resulting probabilities are proportional to these antecedent probabilities (since, if either hypothesis obtained, it would produce the observed series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the antecedent probability of an accidental combination is appreciable but rapidly diminishes with repeated trials, even a small prior probability of e.g. unfairness may soon outweigh chance. When the causal hypothesis is that of an unknown law, its antecedent probability is often inestimable, limiting precise numerical comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical acceptance criterion for new empirical laws from coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of observed coincidences exceeds the average expected from chance by an amount so large that such an accidental occurrence would be extremely uncommon, we have reason to accept the coincidence as due to causation and provisionally receive it as an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact numerical comparison may be impossible when the alternative is an unknown law (antecedent probability unknown), but in practice a sufficiently improbable accumulation of coincidences justifies treating the connection as an empirical law, subject to revision with further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit extension of derivative (empirical) laws to observed collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (e.g. co-occurrence or sequences of effects that result from combinations of causes) generally hold only where the same collocation of primeval causes obtains; thus empirical (derivative) laws are admissible only within the time/place/conditions confirmed by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike ultimate causal laws, derivative laws are more contingent on collocations and are vulnerable to change if collocations vary (e.g. additional counteracting causes, different environments). Extrapolate derivative laws cautiously and only to adjacent/similar cases where necessary collocations are known to hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative uniformities can be frustrated by counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an underlying cause-law is universal, derivative uniformities depending on combinations of causes may fail if a new cause arises that partially or wholly counteracts one of the component causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such frustration does not invalidate the ultimate law, but it does limit the applicability of the derivative uniformity; check for possible counteracting causes when applying or extending empirical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer universal conjunction from observed co-occurrence without checking cause identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The co-occurrence or sequence of two effects (a and b) under some conditions does not imply they are universally conjoined; they may be effects of a common cause A in observed instances but not when produced by different causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before generalizing a co-occurrence into a law, verify whether the same underlying cause is operative in other instances. Example: day followed by night depends on the same cause-combination (sun + rotation); if day arose from a different cause the conjunction might not hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for local/physical asymmetries when mapping 'cases' to probabilities (balls-in-box caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: In physical probability models (e.g. balls in a box), observable local conditions (like relative sizes or positions) affect the actual chance of selection and must be considered rather than treating labels as the sole determinant of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probabilities should reflect the true local conditions that make some outcomes more accessible/favourable (e.g. larger balls more likely to be drawn). When possible, ground probability assignments in the physical/mechanical causes of outcome frequencies rather than naive counts of labels.
